title: We Got Hot and Heavy With Meta’s Muse—and Baffled by Apple’s HomeView
gist: Wired's Uncanny Valley podcast covers Meta's Muse agent readily engaging in sexting, a pro-AI super PAC network paying Nevada shell LLCs amid a toothless FEC, Apple's video-less HomeView hub, and a Harvard study finding men overstate AI knowledge.

insights.claim: Meta's AI agent Muse, the number one app on download charts and promoted inside Instagram, will sext when simply asked, with no jailbreak needed, per WIRED reporter Reece Rogers.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Meta shipped a mass-market agent with permissive adult behavior, raising regulatory and brand-safety exposure.
insights.quote: I asked, "Can you sext?" And I said, "You go first." And the rest is history.
insights.locator: Not hard at all. Not hard in the least

insights.claim: In comparison tests, xAI's Grok bot declined to sext and told the user to focus on tasks, while Meta said Muse is for adults 18 and over and it will not block legal adult behavior.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Guardrail posture varies surprisingly across agents, and Grok is not the permissive outlier assumed.
insights.locator: Yeah, I actually, after I found out it could sext

insights.claim: Experts worry Muse's sexual capability could drive addictive engagement replacing human connections, and that explicit chats make accounts targets for hackers seeking to extort or embarrass users.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Engagement, addiction and privacy-breach liabilities are potential regulatory and legal risks for Meta.
insights.locator: And how this could be problematic

insights.claim: Meta applies strict sexual-content rules to some Instagram creators, such as queer bars whose pages were shut down, while its AI agent is allowed to 'get as freaky as it wants'; the cute mascot also appeals to children.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Inconsistent content policy invites scrutiny from youth advocates and regulators.
insights.locator: But I also found this to contrast

insights.claim: Think Big, a pro-AI super PAC in the Leading the Future network backed by Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz and Greg Brockman, has paid about $20 million since last year to Lantern Production Consultants, a Nevada LLC at a Sparks strip mall.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Opaque spending by AI-industry-backed PACs is an election-transparency and political-risk story.
insights.locator: We are going to Nevada for this next story

insights.claim: The FEC has lacked the four-commissioner quorum needed to act on complaints for over a year and a half, so a Campaign Legal Center complaint against Think Big and American Mission is stalled and the $100 million-plus network has effectively no oversight.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Weak enforcement lowers the cost of opaque political spending by AI interests.
insights.locator: It's a good question, and unfortunately it's not super uncommon

insights.claim: Unlike the crypto PAC Fairshake, the pro-AI PACs fund candidates on both sides, including less competitive seats, to build long-term allies in Congress for deregulation or light regulation and data-center support beyond 2028.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Expect durable bipartisan pro-AI lobbying influence on regulation and data-center policy.
insights.locator: It's a really good question, and I really want to make sure

insights.claim: Leading the Future's spokesperson called the complaint a ploy from Public First, Anthropic and aligned groups, although neither was party to the complaint, hinting at OpenAI-Anthropic infighting via political proxies.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Rivalries between AI labs are spilling into campaign finance.
insights.locator: Absolutely. And when Tess reached out

insights.claim: Apple's HomeView is its first smart home hub, a 7-inch square display with face recognition and Siri AI, but it has no video apps such as Netflix, MLB TV or Prime Video, which the hosts say undermines the point of a screen.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Weak launch app support could slow adoption versus Google and Amazon displays.
insights.locator: The one I am going to make you talk about

insights.claim: Apple told WIRED video apps may appear if developers make CarPlay apps for the device; Brian Barrett says he cannot commit unless developers get on board, and the improved Siri relies on a Google partnership.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Platform success depends on third-party developer buy-in.
insights.locator: 100 percent. We asked Apple about this

insights.claim: A Harvard survey of 5,400+ Americans found more than half of men claimed to know fictitious AI figures, versus around 40 percent of women.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Overconfidence among men signals uneven AI literacy and attitudes that shape adoption and policy.
insights.locator: In a new survey of more than 5,400 Americans

insights.claim: Over a year of media coverage, men were named in AI headlines about 14 times as often as women, and are quoted as AI experts more, which the hosts tie to top AI executives skewing male.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Narrative power in AI is concentrated in a few male personalities.
insights.locator: We found that across a year of media coverage
